abstract.text: Louvain communities (Blondel et al.): each level moves vertices, in index order, to the
neighboring community of greatest modularity gain (staying on a tie, otherwise the greatest
community label), then merges each community into a vertex, while the modularity rises by
more than
. Deterministic: a function of the graph’s vertex numbering and
weights. Parallel edges add; a self-loop counts in degrees and never moves a vertex. O(m)
per sweep.
The constant Potts model of a grouping of the vertices (Traag, Van Dooren and Nesterov
2011): Σ_c [e_c − γ n_c² / 2], e_c the number of edges inside community c (a self-loop is
inside, parallel copies each count) and n_c its number of vertices. O(n + m) after looking
the vertices up.

communities (Ng, Jordan and Weiss 2001): the
eigenvectors of the normalized Laplacian for its
smallest eigenvalues as
columns, each row scaled to unit length (a zero row stays zero), and the rows clustered by

2007) and refined by Lloyd’s iteration until no assignment changes, or 300 iterations. A
cluster left empty takes the row farthest from its center, so there are exactly
communities.

k-clique communities by clique percolation (Palla, Derényi, Farkas and Vicsek 2005): the
unions of k-cliques that can be reached from one another through k-cliques sharing k − 1
vertices. Communities can overlap, and a vertex in no k-clique is in none. Computed from the
maximal cliques of at least k vertices (

least k − 1 vertices. Self-loops and parallel edges are ignored.

eigenvector of each community’s generalized modularity matrix B⁽ᵍ⁾, starting from one
community, while the eigenvalue and the bisection’s modularity gain are positive. The final
partition does not depend on the order of the splits. Parallel edges add; self-loops count

The two-level map equation’s code length L(M) of a grouping of the vertices, in bits
(Rosvall and Bergstrom): the flow is d_α / 2W at each vertex and 1 / 2W along each edge
each way, W the number of edges (a self-loop counts twice in a degree and never leaves a
module); with q_i a community’s exit flow and p_i its vertices’ flow,
L(M) = f(Σ q_i) − 2 Σ f(q_i) − Σ f(p_α) + Σ f(q_i + p_i), f(x) = x log₂ x. 0 without
edges. Takes any grouping, such as a

Walktrap communities (Pons and Latapy 2005): agglomerative clustering by the distance between
the distributions of random walks of
steps, cut where modularity is greatest. Each
vertex gets a self-loop of its mean incident edge weight (1 if it has none) for the walks;
from singletons, the two adjacent communities whose Ward merge raises the walk distance
least, Δσ = (1/n) |C₁||C₂| / (|C₁| + |C₂|) ‖D^(-1/2) (P_C₁ − P_C₂)‖², merge, ties to the
earliest-made pair (vertex numbers first, then merges in order). The partition after the
merges of greatest
is returned, the earliest on a tie. Parallel edges add;
the graph’s own self-loops count in modularity, not in the walks.
Weighted semi-synchronous label propagation: each edge votes with its weight (a zero-weight
edge does not vote).

Weighted asynchronous label propagation with shuffled sweeps and random ties.
Label propagation communities, semi-synchronous (Cordasco and Gargano): every vertex starts
with its own label and repeatedly takes the label most of its edges lead to (each parallel
edge votes; self-loops vote for nothing), keeping its own on a tie, otherwise taking the
greatest; vertices of one color of a greedy coloring update together. Deterministic.

The weighted Louvain levels with shuffled visit orders.
Kernighan–Lin bisection (Kernighan and Lin 1970) from a random balanced split, lowering the
number of edges between the two halves: each pass moves the vertex of greatest gain from
alternate sides (a tie to the vertex whose cost changed least recently, then the lesser
vertex number), each vertex once, and keeps the best prefix of moved pairs while it cuts
fewer edges. Parallel edges add; self-loops never matter. The sizes of the two halves differ
by at most one.
Each community split into its connected components: the partition whose communities are
the components of the subgraphs the communities induce. Louvain can leave a community
disconnected; splitting it never lowers modularity (at any γ ≥ 0) or the constant Potts
model. Empty communities disappear. O(n + m) after looking the vertices up.
Asynchronous fluid communities drawing from the system’s random number generator.
Infomap communities (Rosvall and Bergstrom): the partition of shortest two-level map
equation code length found in
runs, see
. Each run starts from
every vertex alone; a level moves each node, in an order shuffled by
each
sweep, to the neighboring module (or an empty one) that shortens the code length most,
until a sweep moves none, then merges each module into a node, until no modules merge.
The run is then tuned while that shortens the code length, alternately from its modules on
the vertices and from its modules on their submodules (each module split by a run on it
alone), and the single module wins when it is shorter than every run. Parallel edges add; a
self-loop adds to its vertex’s flow and never leaves a module. A graph without edges
gives every vertex alone. O(m) per sweep.
Girvan–Newman communities: the successively finer partitions found by removing, again and
again, the edge of greatest betweenness (
), recomputed after
each removal. A tie goes to the least edge position; parallel copies share their pairs’
paths, and self-loops are never removed and never matter. The sequence is lazy: each
partition is computed when iteration reaches it.

the two adjacent communities whose merge raises modularity most (ties to the least pair of
vertex numbers), while it does not lower it. Deterministic. O(m d log n), d the depth of the
merge tree.
